scenarios.description: For a single offer record, the semantic facts an accessibility label could be built from (title presence, retailer known/unknown, price/currency known/unknown, commerce type retail/resale/unknown) must be programmatically available; exact label copy is not asserted here, only the underlying facts plus one provisional example.

expectedOutcome.provisionalExampleSentence: PROVISIONAL PRESENTATION TEMPLATE: 'Wool Blend Overcoat, $395.00, from Nordstrom.'

scenarios.description: For a Where-to-Buy-style list of N offers, the semantic fact 'number of purchase options: N' must be programmatically available; exact phrasing is provisional.

expectedOutcome.provisionalExamplePhrase: PROVISIONAL PRESENTATION TEMPLATE: '3 ways to buy this item.'

scenarios.description: For an offer carrying a watchCapability value, the semantic fact 'watch available: true/false' must be programmatically available; exact phrasing is provisional.

expectedOutcome.provisionalExamplePhrase: PROVISIONAL PRESENTATION TEMPLATE: 'Watch available for price updates.'

scenarios.description: A bare canonical merchant URL with no query string at all is the simplest true case: no attribution, no tracking, nothing to preserve or strip.

A candidate affiliateUrl carries embedded basic-auth-style credentials. This must be rejected as a destination outright — attribution safety checking is a URL-safety problem, not a URL-rewriting problem, and this corpus does not invent a scrubbing mechanism that doesn't exist in source.

An offer with affiliateUrl explicitly null. This is the truthful, common case: no attribution mechanism exists in source (AFFILIATE_AUTHORITY: ABSENT), so 'no attribution' must remain 'no attribution' rather than being backfilled with anything.
An ordinary, non-tracking query parameter (e.g. a color/size selector) on a retailer URL must be preserved untouched when selecting the Shop destination.

A safe-looking https redirect URL through a third-party redirect host is a URL-safety case, not an attribution case: it may be opened if it passes isSafeCommerceUrl, but that alone must never be presented as proof of governed affiliate attribution.

A URL carries an ordinary-looking UTM/tracking query string that the PROVIDER supplied. This must not be interpreted as governed K Scan attribution (since none exists) — it is preserved as part of the URL, but the corpus must not label it 'K Scan attribution' or assert revenue tracking is occurring.
No authenticity-verification field exists anywhere in source, so an 'Authentic' claim is not licensed, even on a resale listing where authenticity concerns are most salient.

expectedOutcome.reason: commerceType only distinguishes retail vs. resale channel; it is not an authenticity signal, and no separate authentication/verification field exists on any production commerce shape.

scenarios.description: No field on this record, or on any client-consumed commerce shape, asserts that this price is the lowest available across retailers, so a 'Best Price' claim is not licensed.

expectedOutcome.reason: There is no cross-retailer price-comparison authority client-side; this record carries only its own retailer's price, with no field comparing it to any other retailer's offer for the same item.

scenarios.description: The same missing cross-retailer price-comparison authority means a 'Cheapest' claim is not licensed either, regardless of wording.

expectedOutcome.reason: There is no cross-retailer price-comparison authority client-side; a lower number on one retailer's own record does not license a superlative claim about every other retailer's price for the same item.

scenarios.description: CanonicalPurchaseOption/PurchaseOption/WatchCandidate shelf records carry no price-freshness timestamp at all, so 'Current Price' is not a licensable claim from those shapes today; a Watchlist-style record that DOES carry a lastCheckedAt/observedAt timestamp could license a narrower 'last checked' style claim (not 'current'), but that nuance does not license the word 'Current' either, since even a recent check timestamp doesn't make a price true at this instant.

expectedOutcome.reason: This record has the shape of a CanonicalPurchaseOption/PurchaseOption, neither of which carries any freshness timestamp field; RP-110 governs correctness of the displayed number/currency but says nothing about how recently the price was observed.

scenarios.description: A high matchScore alone does not license an 'Exact Match' claim: matchScore measures visual/text similarity, not verified product identity.

expectedOutcome.reason: matchScore is a similarity score, not an identity assertion; no field on this or any production shape asserts exact SKU/GTIN/UPC identity between the scanned item and this listing, so no matchScore value -- even 0.94 -- licenses an 'Exact Match' label.

scenarios.description: Free-text availability that doesn't match a recognized literal must not be presented as 'In Stock' -- only an exact match to a known in-stock string licenses that label.

expectedOutcome.reason: availability is free text; only exact matches to 'in_stock'/'in stock'/'available' normalize to the 'In Stock' label. This string matches none of those, so availability is effectively unknown and must not be presented as In Stock.

scenarios.description: No partner or affiliate-program relationship exists in source, so an 'Official Partner' claim is not licensed.

expectedOutcome.reason: AFFILIATE_AUTHORITY is ABSENT: no affiliate ID, click ID, tracking parameter, or network/partner ID is ever minted anywhere in source, so no partner/affiliate-program relationship exists to license this claim.

scenarios.description: No boolean or field anywhere -- client or backend -- asserts retailer verification or authentication, so a 'Verified Retailer' claim is not licensed.

expectedOutcome.reason: No 'verified retailer' / 'official partner' / 'authenticated' boolean exists anywhere in source; 'retailer' is a bare string field, and no verification step or authority ever populates or checks it.

scenarios.description: A third-party affiliate-redirect-shaped domain is a safe https URL (no embedded credentials, not a private host) but is not a direct retailer identity -- retailer identity stays unknown/unresolved from the URL alone, unlike dom-exact-merchant-domain.
A URL carrying embedded username:password-style credentials is rejected outright, regardless of protocol or host.
A clean https URL on a retailer's own bare apex domain is a safe URL and resolves to a known retailer identity.
An otherwise well-formed retailer URL is rejected solely because its scheme is http, not https -- contrast with dom-exact-merchant-domain, the identical host over https, which passes.
A string that does not parse as a URL at all is rejected outright and never reaches retailer classification.

A generic shared redirect host and a generic shared CDN/image host, both used by many unrelated retailers, cannot establish retailer identity from the hostname alone -- both remain safe URLs but resolve to unknown-retailer.

A legitimate retailer https URL carrying a long signed-looking query string plus ordinary utm_ tracking parameters is still safe: isSafeCommerceUrl only inspects protocol, embedded username/password, and hostname, and never rejects on query-string content -- contrast with dom-credential-shaped-url, where basic-auth-style user:pass@ credentials embedded IN the URL (a different, rejected risk class) cause rejection.

www, regional, and marketplace subdomains of the same retailer all resolve to the same retailer identity and are all safe; per Section 16 these subdomain variants must not be conflated with 'unknown retailer' just because the hostname isn't the bare apex domain.
A domain with no recognizable retailer signal at all is still a safe https URL but resolves to no known retailer identity.

A general async-safety property for stale/duplicate/late commerce callbacks: the UI must reflect only the latest request's result, must not double-apply a duplicate response, and must not apply a late response to a candidate/screen that has moved on.

expectedOutcome.latestOnly: only req-2's result is applied to cand-race-1's card, even though req-1 (issued earlier) resolves later at 300ms
expectedOutcome.noDoubleApply: req-2's duplicate delivery at 150ms must not be applied a second time
expectedOutcome.noApplyAfterNavigateAway: no response arriving after userNavigatedAwayAtMs (400ms) may be applied to a screen/candidate the user has left

scenarios.description: A commerce fetch fails with a non-no_results errorType (e.g. provider_error); this must render as a distinct error state, never conflated with a genuine no-match.
A commerce fetch is still in flight; this must render as a loading/pending state, not as empty and not as an error.

A listing whose availability indicates it is gone must be shown as unavailable truthfully, without crashing; Watch behavior on an unavailable listing is described conservatively since it was not independently verified.

expectedOutcome.watchOnUnavailableListing: SYNTHETIC nuance — not asserted here whether Watch could still be offered to notify on restock; only the safe, verified facts are asserted (no crash, availability shown truthfully)

scenarios.description: Five otherwise-valid offer records, each missing exactly one required field (title, retailer, imageUrl, price, productUrl), must each degrade safely without crashing and without fabricating a stand-in value for the missing field.

expectedOutcome.rendering: neutral retailer placeholder shown, no claim of a specific real retailer name
no-image-state (placeholder graphic, not a broken image)
no price shown; not rendered as $0.00 or any other invented amount

scenarios.description: A commerce fetch completes with a genuinely empty result set; this must render as an empty state, not an error state.
An error card marked retryable: false must not offer a retry action.
An error card marked retryable: true must offer a retry action.
An offer whose only productUrl is unsafe (embedded credentials) must render with the Shop action suppressed, not crash.
A listing with watchCapability: 'unsupported' must not offer a Watch action; this is a normal, expected, non-error state.

Negative control: if candidate cand-jacket-1's bestMatch.productUrl were ever rendered under candidate cand-skirt-1's Shop action, that must be treated as a bug, since the real Map-keyed-by-candidateId return shape makes this impossible when implemented correctly.
Three candidates where the middle one errors; the other two candidates' ready cards with real bestMatch data are entirely unaffected by that error.
Three detected garments (jacket, skirt, boots) each produce their own independent commerce card; no card's data is shared or merged across candidates.
Visual/perceptual image similarity alone (no shared exact identity field at all) must never license grouping — this corpus does not endorse an image-hash-based matching heuristic as identity.
Same brand and same color description is still not enough to prove identity — many products from one brand share both.

Same brand, IDENTICAL marketing title, two different retailers, two different colorways (carried only in the variant field, which the title text does not mention). canonicalProductKey reads only brand+title, never variant/color, so this is EXACTLY the shape of listing the real, dormant algorithm would collapse together -- and exactly the shape the corpus's doctrine requires stay separate absent an exact identity match.
Two entirely different products in the same category (e.g. two different sneakers) must never be grouped merely for sharing a category.
Two products in the same model family (e.g. two different generations/versions of the same sneaker line) must not be grouped as the same product.

Two listings sharing the exact same product photo but different SKU/productId values must stay separate — a shared stock photo is not proof of shared identity (retailers frequently reuse manufacturer stock photography across different variants or even different products).
Two listings from the SAME retailer with similar names must still stay separate absent an exact ID match — same-retailer proximity is not identity either.

A one-character title typo between two listings (e.g. a transposed letter) must not be treated as proof they are the same listing at two retailers — a fuzzy/edit-distance match is exactly the kind of implicit identity this corpus forbids.
Two visually similar but genuinely different garments from different brands must never be grouped just because they look alike in a photo.
Mutation of 'aff-no-attribution-null-field': attribution-fabricated must be flagged, not silently accepted.

expectedOutcome.doctrineViolated: Section 25: AFFILIATE_AUTHORITY is ABSENT; attribution must never be asserted present where no mechanism exists

scenarios.description: Mutation of 'ri-brand-known-seller-unknown': brand-as-retailer must be flagged, not silently accepted.

expectedOutcome.doctrineViolated: Section 14: brand must never be displayed as retailer

scenarios.description: Mutation of 'aff-credential-shaped-param-rejected': credential-shaped-url-not-rejected must be flagged, not silently accepted.

expectedOutcome.doctrineViolated: Section 16/25: a URL with embedded credentials must be rejected, never opened

scenarios.description: Mutation of 'price-missing-currency': currency-fabricated must be flagged, not silently accepted.

expectedOutcome.doctrineViolated: RP-110 / Section 18: an undeclared currency must never be guessed as USD or rendered with a '$'

scenarios.description: Mutation of 'mng-same-brand-similar-title': fuzzy-identity-grouped must be flagged, not silently accepted.

expectedOutcome.doctrineViolated: Section 28: same-brand-similar-title must stay separate; this is the exact canonicalProductKey risk in Finding F2

scenarios.description: Mutation of 'aff-ordinary-query-param-preserved': legitimate-parameter-stripped must be flagged, not silently accepted.

expectedOutcome.doctrineViolated: Section 25: a legitimate, already-present URL parameter must be preserved untouched, not silently stripped

scenarios.description: Mutation of 'wtb-multiple-retailers-order-preserved': order-not-preserved must be flagged, not silently accepted.

expectedOutcome.doctrineViolated: Section 31/38: source order must be preserved; sorting by price/commission is forbidden

scenarios.description: Mutation of 'shop-id-per-offer-independent': cross-offer-shop-destination-leakage must be flagged, not silently accepted.

expectedOutcome.doctrineViolated: Section 24: Shop on offer A must never open offer B's URL

scenarios.description: Mutation of 'dom-unknown-domain': unknown-domain-falsely-resolved must be flagged, not silently accepted.

expectedOutcome.doctrineViolated: Section 16: an unrecognizable domain must resolve to unknown-retailer, never a guessed known retailer

scenarios.description: Mutation of 'watch-id-per-offer-independent': cross-offer-watch-identity-leakage must be flagged, not silently accepted.

expectedOutcome.doctrineViolated: Section 23/DEF-WL-07: watching offer A must never carry offer B's identity

scenarios.description: Mutation of 'ri-stable-retailer-key-fixture-values': logo-identity-mismatch must be flagged, not silently accepted.

expectedOutcome.doctrineViolated: a retailerKey's associated logo/identity must match the retailer actually being displayed

scenarios.description: An already-provider-formatted price string with no separate currency field passes through unchanged, because it is not purely numeric and is not one of the null-triggering empty/zero literals.
A finite positive numeric price with a valid EUR currency code formats with the euro symbol.
A finite positive numeric price with a valid GBP currency code formats with the pound symbol.
A price given as a JS number and the identical price given as a numeric-looking string both parse to the same numeric value and produce an identical formatted string, proving type-agnostic parsing.

A non-numeric passthrough string ('free shipping') is returned unchanged via the text-passthrough rule, while a zero price and a negative price both format to null via the non-positive-numeric rule -- these are two different code branches and must not be confused.
A finite positive numeric price with no currency at all formats as the bare number with no symbol, no code, and no locale guess.
A null price with a currency present still formats to null: currency alone never implies a price.

A whole-value JPY price and a USD price with more than two source decimal places both go through the same Intl.NumberFormat currency-style call, which applies each currency's own default fraction-digit rounding rather than always forcing two decimals.

A well-formed-looking but non-real 3-letter currency code passes shape validation, then is accepted directly by Intl.NumberFormat (which does not validate against the real ISO-4217 list either) and rendered using the code itself as the symbol, rather than being treated as unknown.
A finite positive numeric price with a valid USD currency code formats via Intl.NumberFormat currency style.

SKU, GTIN, UPC, and EAN fields do not exist anywhere in this app's real production commerce types. This fixture documents that absence explicitly so the corpus does not silently invent these fields elsewhere.

No field in production source establishes a governed, stable identity that is comparable ACROSS retailers for the same physical product. This is the single most important input to the Grouping Readiness verdict.
An offer with no productId, no SKU, and no other identity field at all — this must be handled as 'no stable identity', not silently treated as identical to any other offer with the same title/brand.

A provider-issued product ID exists on the offer, but it is scoped to that single provider/listing — it must never be treated as a universal identity that would justify matching it against a DIFFERENT retailer's product ID for the 'same' item.
A valid-looking image URL that fails to load at render time (a runtime image-load event, not a URL-shape problem) must not crash the screen and must fall back to a safe empty/placeholder image state.
An image URL string that isn't a valid https URL is treated as absent, not displayed as broken markup.
When no image field is present at all, the product record must fail safely to a no-image/placeholder display state rather than rendering broken markup.
When imageUrl, image_url, thumbnail, and thumbnailUrl are all present with different values, imageUrl wins: the alias chain tries imageUrl first and returns on the first non-empty normalized result.

An image URL carrying a long signed-token-shaped query string (?sig=...&expires=...) is actually REJECTED (resolved to null, treated as absent), not kept: the persisted image alias chain runs every image URL through the same normalizePersistedCommerceUrl() used for purchase-option destination URLs, and that function treats 'sig' and 'expires' as disqualifying query keys for ANY persisted commerce URL, image URLs included.
A clean https image URL with no sensitive-looking query parameters is used directly as the displayable product image.
A retail offer and a Poshmark resale offer for the same garment are shown side by side, with neither ranked above the other on the basis of commerceType.
A Poshmark resale listing explicitly carries commerceType: 'resale', the only provider in the real system that ever sets this field.
A resale offer whose availability signal indicates the listing is gone normalizes to an Out of Stock label rather than being silently dropped.
A resale offer carries condition-like information inside the generic free-text availability field, since no dedicated structured condition enum exists in the real source.
A normal retail offer from an ordinary provider (e.g. Serper-sourced) carries no commerceType field at all — absence is the realistic representation of retail, not an explicit 'retail' string.
An offer from a generic/ambiguous provider has no commerceType field and no other signal that would let it be attributed to either retail or resale — it must not be defaulted to retail.
A record with a known brand but no retailer, merchant, store, or source field at all must report the seller as UNKNOWN — never substitute the brand.

Brand, retailer, and commerce provider are three independent facts and must never collapse into one another: a Nike jacket sold by Farfetch, surfaced through provider-X, must report retailer = Farfetch, not Nike and not provider-X.

Reproduces Finding F1 (Build 35 convergence update, post-#339): the exact same raw commerce record, run through the four real retailer-resolution call sites that exist in source today, now produces the SAME result for 'who is the retailer' across all four -- Commerce V2 (PR #339) removed the brand fallback from the two call sites that used to substitute it. This scenario now documents the post-fix behavior for regression-tracking: all four call sites are internally consistent, but none yet meet the doctrine target of leaving retailer genuinely unknown when only a provider/source string is available.

callSites.name: getRetailer
callSites.violation: CLOSED (Commerce V2, #339): brand fallback removed. Remaining violation: substitutes provider name for retailer, same softer category as the other two call sites

callSites.name: normalizePurchaseOptions (persisted)
callSites.violation: CLOSED (Commerce V2, #339): brand fallback removed, per the seller-truth repair comment at this call site. Remaining violation: substitutes provider name for retailer, same softer category as the other two call sites

callSites.name: mapRawProductToPurchaseOption
callSites.violation: substitutes provider name for retailer (unchanged by #339, still not a verified retailer)

callSites.name: mapLegacyToV2 similarFinds mapping
callSites.violation: same as above; still not the one call site that leaves retailer genuinely unknown in this particular input (that path only leaves it unknown when source is ALSO absent)

scenarios.description: When a provider names a merchant but no explicit retailer field, the merchant IS the seller — this is an audited semantic mapping (merchant == retailer-of-record), not a brand fallback.
A record with a known commerce provider/source but no retailer, brand, merchant, or store field must never silently display the provider name as if it were the retailer.

Demonstrates the corpus's retailer-key fixture convention: this corpus uses stable lowercase-kebab retailerKey values (e.g. 'nordstrom', 'farfetch') as test data ONLY. It does not create or own a production retailer registry, logo mapping, or RetailerIdentity component — those belong to Commerce V2 (Section 15).

expectedOutcome.usageNote: retailerKey is a stable fixture-data convention only

scenarios.description: IF a governed, cross-retailer-comparable exact product identifier existed (it does not, in production, today — see Finding F2), grouping two DIFFERENT retailers' offers under one product by that exact ID would be safe. This fixture demonstrates what safe cross-retailer grouping WOULD look like, using a clearly-labeled hypothetical field, so Commerce V2 has a concrete target shape to build toward without this corpus fabricating that the capability exists now.

Two raw listing entries with the IDENTICAL (retailer, productUrl, price, size, variant, productId) tuple must collapse into ONE purchase option. This is a real, currently-shipped exact-identity mechanism — not a proposal.

10 deterministically generated offers exercising a realistic mix of Retail/Resale, known/unknown retailer, logo authority, watch eligibility, known/unknown currency, and exact-group/must-not-group candidates.

25 deterministically generated offers exercising a realistic mix of Retail/Resale, known/unknown retailer, logo authority, watch eligibility, known/unknown currency, and exact-group/must-not-group candidates.

50 deterministically generated offers exercising a realistic mix of Retail/Resale, known/unknown retailer, logo authority, watch eligibility, known/unknown currency, and exact-group/must-not-group candidates.

Two offers, each with its own distinct productUrl. Tapping Shop on offer A must open offer A's URL; tapping Shop on offer B must open offer B's URL. Neither offer's safe URL may be substituted for the other's.

Offer A's only URL is unsafe (http, not https) while sibling offer B has a perfectly good https URL. Shop on offer A must be suppressed entirely — it must NOT silently open offer B's URL just because a safe URL exists somewhere in the list.

Three offers for the same detected garment, each at a different retailer (two watch-eligible retail offers, one non-watch-eligible resale offer). Watching offer A must carry only offer A's identity (canonicalUrl, retailer, price) — never offer B's or C's.
A listing record that predates the watchCapability field entirely (field absent, not merely falsy) must not be treated as watchable — absence is never inferred as eligibility.

expectedOutcome.reasoning: watchCapability field absent, not defaulted to refreshable_listing or unsupported

scenarios.description: A real retail offer whose URL matches the registered, enabled Farfetch provider is watch-eligible.
A Poshmark resale offer is not watch-eligible because Poshmark, like every provider except Farfetch and KicksCrew, has no re-observation-by-identity adapter.

A record where type is 'similar' (a similar-style web link, not a real offer) nonetheless carries watchCapability: 'refreshable_listing' by data error; the client-side eligibility check does not independently re-verify type==='retail', it trusts the server-set watchCapability field completely — this is a documented tension/gap between the two independent check functions, not an observed real-world case.

expectedOutcome.computedFrom: watchCapability field only, type field not re-checked downstream

scenarios.description: A real retail offer from a generic Serper-sourced URL is not watch-eligible, even though it is a genuine retail offer, because its provider has no re-observation-by-identity adapter.
Five offers, all from a single retailer, is the extreme case of concentration; no correction is applied, the same as the skewed case.
Eight offers spread evenly (two each) across four different retailers is a balanced concentration; no correction or rebalancing is applied and source order is preserved.
Ten offers where eight come from one retailer and two from others is a skewed concentration; no rebalancing or correction is applied, and the skew must remain visible/testable.
Four offers from four different retailers, in a specific deliberate order, must be shown in exactly that order — never re-sorted by price or commission.
A Where to Buy list with exactly one offer from one retailer.
A mix of two retail offers and one Poshmark resale offer, order preserved as given, with neither commerceType ranked above the other.
Three offers from the same retailer, representing different sizes or variants, are all shown rather than collapsed or deduped.

expectedOutcome.reasoning: distinct variants (different sizes), not exact duplicate listings

scenarios.description: One of three offers has no resolvable retailer field at all; it must still be included in the list, shown as unknown, not silently dropped and not fabricated as a fake retailer name.
